title: Dementia Risk Factors Vary Sharply Across Countries, Lancet Study Finds
excerpt: A new analysis of 214,000 older adults across 14 countries reveals that while the risk factors for dementia differ dramatically by region, they cluster in strikingly similar patterns worldwide.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Low education affects 85.6% of older adults in China, but only 12% in the U.S.
  • Over 50% of individuals in all countries studied had at least two modifiable dementia risk factors.
  • Up to 45% of dementia cases could be prevented by addressing 14 modifiable risk factors.
  • Interventions must be tailored to each country's specific dementia risk factors for effectiveness.

  • Low education affected 85.6% of older adults in China but only 12% in the U.S., while obesity rates were 44.9% in the U.S. versus 13.3% in India — underscoring the need for region-specific dementia prevention.
  • More than 50% of individuals in all 14 countries studied had at least two modifiable dementia risk factors, with cardiovascular conditions, risky behaviours, and sensory impairments clustering together consistently.
  • Up to 45% of dementia cases globally could be prevented by addressing 14 modifiable risk factors, but interventions must be tailored to each country's specific burden rather than using a one-size-fits-all model.
  • For immigrant populations, clinicians should consider patients' lifetime exposures from their countries of origin rather than assuming Western risk patterns apply to everyone.

A sweeping cross-national analysis published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity has mapped how 12 modifiable risk factors for dementia vary across 14 countries and regions, revealing stark differences that researchers say should reshape how governments and healthcare systems approach prevention.

The study, led by Emma Nichols, an epidemiologist at the University of Southern California's Schaeffer Institute, analysed harmonised survey data from more than 214,000 adults aged 50 and older across Ireland, the United States, England, Northern Ireland, four European sub-regions, South Korea, Mexico, China, Malaysia, Brazil, and India. Data were collected between 2009 and 2023 through 11 nationally representative ageing studies.

Dramatic Gaps Between Nations

The findings paint a picture of deeply uneven risk. Low formal education — one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for dementia — affected 85.6% of older adults in China and 76.7% in India, compared with just 12% in the United States. Obesity showed the reverse pattern: 44.9% of Americans met the obesity threshold versus 13.3% of Indians and 6.2% of South Koreans.

Hypertension prevalence ranged from 28.5% in India to 55% in the United States, with Mexico (53.1%) and Brazil (49%) showing higher rates than other countries at similar income levels. Depression was highest in Eastern Europe (37.6%) and China (37.2%), while vision loss was a dominant risk factor in India (69.7%) and Brazil (49.6%) — far exceeding rates in high-income countries.

"Differences in the prevalence of risk factors across contexts suggest that different approaches are likely needed to best address dementia burden in these different settings."

— Emma Nichols, PhD, University of Southern California

Similar Clusters, Different Priorities

Despite these differences, the researchers found that risk factors cluster in remarkably similar ways worldwide. Cardiovascular conditions — hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, and in some cases obesity — grouped together across all 14 settings. Smoking and excessive alcohol use consistently appeared in the same cluster. Hearing loss, vision loss, and low education also frequently co-occurred.

More than half of individuals in every country studied carried at least two risk factors simultaneously. Mexico and Brazil had the highest levels of co-occurring factors, at 35% and 34% of the total risk factors measured, while South Korea had the lowest at 21%.

"Similarities in the patterning of risk factors across studies suggest that despite observed differences, interventions and policies across contexts could use similar designs to account for risk factor clustering patterns," Nichols said.

Why This Matters for Prevention

The 2024 Lancet Commission on dementia reported that 45% of all dementia cases globally are attributable to 14 modifiable factors spanning early life, midlife, and later years. With more than 57 million people worldwide living with dementia and nearly 10 million new diagnoses annually, the potential impact of targeted prevention is enormous.

But the new study makes clear that a universal prevention strategy would miss the mark. Addressing low education could be transformative in China and India, where it dominates the risk landscape. In the U.S. and Western Europe, however, obesity, social isolation, and cardiovascular management are more pressing targets. In India and China, cardiovascular risk factors like diabetes and hypertension were more common among highly educated individuals — the opposite of the pattern seen in wealthy nations.

Implications for Immigrant Health

Dung Trinh, an internist and chief medical officer at the Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, told Medical News Today that the findings carry direct relevance for clinicians treating immigrant populations in high-income countries.

"Immigrants may arrive with different lifetime exposures, educational opportunities, health-care access, cultural norms, and levels of awareness or treatment of conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, hearing loss, or depression," Trinh said. "Country-level findings should never be used to stereotype an individual patient, but they can help clinicians ask better questions."

"For patients, I think the hopeful message is that brain health can be supported over time. We cannot eliminate every risk, and not every case of dementia is preventable, but many of the same steps that protect the heart and overall health may also protect the brain."

— Raphael Wald, PsyD, Marcus Neuroscience Institute

This week, the World Health Organization released updated guidelines on dementia prevention, adding air pollution reduction as a recommendation for the first time and reinforcing the role of managing blood pressure, diabetes, hearing loss, and cholesterol. The new Lancet study provides the granular country-level data needed to turn those broad guidelines into locally relevant action plans.

What Comes Next

Global Dementia Prevention Potential
›57 million people live with dementia globally.
›10 million new dementia diagnoses occur annually.
›45% of dementia cases linked to 14 modifiable factors.
›Targeted prevention strategies are crucial for effectiveness.

The study's authors acknowledged limitations, including reliance on self-reported diagnoses for conditions like hypertension and diabetes, which may undercount prevalence in countries with limited healthcare access. India's LASI survey lacked comparable alcohol consumption data, and some datasets dated back to 2009.

Still, the research represents the most comprehensive cross-national comparison of dementia risk factor prevalence to date. The team called for expanded harmonised data collection, standardised biomarker measurement, and — critically — cluster-tailored multidomain trials that test whether interventions designed around the specific risk factor patterns of a given population produce better results than generic prevention programmes.
